questions.question_text: In a herd, $1$ newborn calf in every $5$ is a twin. Which device best models whether one newborn calf is a twin?

options.text: A spinner with $5$ equal sectors, with one sector labelled 'twin'.
A six-sided die, with a roll of $1$ meaning 'twin'.
options.why: Picks a familiar device without checking that $\frac{1}{6}$ does not match $\frac{1}{5}$.

options.text: A coin, with heads meaning 'twin'.
options.why: Uses a device with only $2$ equally likely outcomes for an event of probability $\frac{1}{5}$.

options.text: A spinner with $5$ equal sectors, with four sectors labelled 'twin'.
options.why: Assigns the sectors the wrong way round, giving a probability of $\frac{4}{5}$ instead of $\frac{1}{5}$.

questions.solution_text:
The probability of a twin is $\frac{1}{5}$, so the device needs $5$ equally likely outcomes.
One of the five sectors must stand for a twin.
A spinner with $5$ equal sectors and one sector labelled 'twin' models the situation.

questions.question_text: A goalkeeper saves $40\%$ of penalty shots. A simulation uses random digits from $0$ to $9$, one digit for each shot. Which assignment models the situation correctly?

options.text: $0, 1, 2, 3$ mean a save; $4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9$ mean a goal.
$0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ mean a save; $5, 6, 7, 8, 9$ mean a goal.
options.why: Splits the ten digits into two halves, giving a saving probability of $0.5$ instead of $0.4$.

options.text: $1, 2, 3, 4$ mean a save; $5, 6, 7, 8, 9$ mean a goal.
options.why: Starts counting at $1$ and leaves the digit $0$ unassigned, so the digits no longer model all shots.

options.text: $0, 1, 2, 3$ mean a goal; $4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9$ mean a save.
options.why: Swaps the two events, giving the goalkeeper a saving probability of $0.6$.

questions.solution_text:
The digits $0$ to $9$ give $10$ equally likely outcomes.
$40\%$ of $10$ is $4$, so $4$ digits must stand for a save.
Let $0, 1, 2, 3$ mean a save and let $4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9$ mean a goal.

questions.question_text: About $1$ in every $4$ cereal boxes contains a toy. Ella models one box by rolling a six-sided die and calling a roll of $1$ or $2$ a toy. Why is her simulation unsuitable?

options.text: It gives a probability of $\frac{1}{3}$ for a toy instead of $\frac{1}{4}$.
It gives a probability of $\frac{1}{2}$ for a toy instead of $\frac{1}{4}$.
options.why: Counts the two chosen faces against four outcomes rather than against the die's six faces.

options.text: It uses two faces for the toy when a simulation must always use exactly one outcome.
options.why: Believes an event must be modelled by a single outcome rather than by a matching share of them.

options.text: A die can never be used in a simulation, because only coins and spinners are random devices.
options.why: Rules out a whole class of devices instead of checking whether its probabilities match.

questions.solution_text:
Two faces out of six give $P(\text{toy}) = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$.
The real probability is $\frac{1}{4}$, and $\frac{1}{3} \neq \frac{1}{4}$.
The die makes a toy more likely than it really is, so the simulation is unsuitable.

questions.question_text:
A simulation of newborn calves uses a coin, with heads meaning 'female'. The results of $24$ trials are shown, where F means female and M means male.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline F & M & F & F & M & M & F & M & F & F & M & F \\\hline M & F & F & F & F & M & F & M & M & F & F & M \\\hline\end{array}$
Estimate, as a fraction in simplest form, the probability that a calf is female.

options.why: Counted the $10$ M results instead of the $14$ F results, giving $\frac{10}{24} = \frac{5}{12}$.
Halved the numerator of $\frac{14}{24}$ but left the number of trials unchanged.
Counted the $10$ M results and then halved only the numerator of $\frac{10}{24}$.

questions.solution_text:
There are $24$ trials and F appears $14$ times.
$\text{Estimated probability} = \frac{14}{24}$
$= \frac{7}{12}$

questions.question_text:
A goalkeeper saves $30\%$ of penalty shots. A simulation uses random digits where $0, 1, 2$ mean a save. One trial is $4$ digits, modelling four shots. Eight trials gave these digits.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline 5310 & 8794 & 2065 & 4471 \\\hline 9382 & 1250 & 6738 & 4956 \\\hline\end{array}$
Estimate, as a fraction in simplest form, the probability that at least $2$ of $4$ shots are saved.

options.why: Counted every trial containing at least one save, rather than at least two saves.
Counted the $9$ saved shots out of the $32$ digits instead of counting whole trials.
Divided the $3$ successful trials by the $32$ digits instead of by the $8$ trials.

questions.solution_text:
Count the digits $0$, $1$ and $2$ in each group of four.
$5310$ has $2$ saves, $8794$ has $0$, $2065$ has $2$ and $4471$ has $1$.
$9382$ has $1$, $1250$ has $3$, $6738$ has $0$ and $4956$ has $0$.
Three of the eight trials gave at least $2$ saves.
$\text{Estimated probability} = \frac{3}{8}$

questions.question_text: Two students estimate the probability that a cereal box contains a toy. Rita simulates $40$ boxes and gets $6$ toys. Sam simulates $400$ boxes and gets $74$ toys. Whose estimate is more likely to be close to the true probability, and why?

options.text: Sam's, because a larger number of trials makes the relative frequency more likely to be close to the true probability.
Rita's, because fewer trials leave less room for the results to vary.
options.why: Reverses the Law of Large Numbers, treating fewer trials as the more reliable estimate.

options.text: Rita's, because her results give the simpler fraction.
options.why: Judges the estimate by how neat the fraction looks instead of by the number of trials.

options.text: Neither, because a simulation is equally accurate however many trials are run.
options.why: Ignores that the relative frequency only settles down as the number of trials grows.

questions.solution_text:
Rita's estimate is $\frac{6}{40} = 0.15$ and Sam's is $\frac{74}{400} = 0.185$.
By the Law of Large Numbers, the relative frequency approaches the true probability as the number of trials increases.
Sam ran ten times as many trials, so his estimate is more likely to be close to the true probability.

questions.question_text: A simulation models rainy days using digits where $0, 1, 2$ mean a rainy day, so the probability built into it is $0.3$. In $250$ trials the simulation gave $68$ rainy days. Which statement best describes this result?

options.text: The estimate is $0.272$, close to $0.3$ but not equal to it, which is expected from a simulation.
The estimate is $0.272$, so the simulation must have been set up incorrectly.
options.why: Treats any gap between an estimate and the built-in probability as a fault in the design.

options.text: The estimate is $0.68$, far from $0.3$, so the simulation has failed.
options.why: Reads the number of rainy days as the probability instead of dividing by the $250$ trials.

options.text: The estimate is $0.3$, because that is the probability the simulation was built on.
options.why: Reports the built-in probability rather than the relative frequency the trials actually produced.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{Estimated probability} = \frac{68}{250}$
$= 0.272$
A simulation gives an estimate, so a small gap from $0.3$ is expected rather than a sign of an error.

questions.question_text: A striker scores $75\%$ of her penalty shots. Which of these is a correct design for a simulation estimating the probability that she scores all of her next $3$ shots?

options.text: Spin a spinner with $4$ equal sectors, $3$ of them meaning 'goal'; one trial is $3$ spins, and a trial succeeds when all $3$ are goals.
Spin a spinner with $4$ equal sectors, $3$ of them meaning 'goal'; one trial is $1$ spin, and a trial succeeds when it is a goal.
options.why: Makes one trial a single shot, so the simulation never models three shots in a row.

options.text: Spin a spinner with $3$ equal sectors, $1$ of them meaning 'goal'; one trial is $3$ spins, and a trial succeeds when all $3$ are goals.
options.why: Confuses the $3$ shots with the number of sectors, giving a scoring probability of $\frac{1}{3}$.

options.text: Toss a coin $3$ times, with heads meaning 'goal'; a trial succeeds when all $3$ tosses are heads.
options.why: Uses a device giving a scoring probability of $0.5$ for a striker who scores $75\%$ of the time.

questions.solution_text:
A spinner with $4$ equal sectors and $3$ of them labelled 'goal' gives $P(\text{goal}) = \frac{3}{4} = 75\%$.
One trial must model all three shots, so one trial is $3$ spins.
The trial succeeds only when all $3$ spins are goals.

questions.question_text:
A goalkeeper saves $50\%$ of penalty shots. A simulation uses a coin, where a head means a save, and one trial is $4$ tosses modelling four shots. Ten trials gave these results.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline HHTT & THTH & HHHT & TTTH & HTHH \\\hline TTHT & HHTH & THTT & HHHH & TTHH \\\hline\end{array}$
Estimate, as a fraction in simplest form, the probability that the goalkeeper saves more than half of the four shots.

options.why: Reads 'more than half of four' as $2$ or more saves instead of $3$ or more.
Counted all $22$ saved shots out of the $40$ tosses instead of counting whole trials.
Counted only the trial in which every one of the four shots was saved.

questions.solution_text:
More than half of four shots means $3$ or $4$ heads in a trial.
$HHHT$, $HTHH$, $HHTH$ and $HHHH$ each have at least $3$ heads.
That is $4$ of the $10$ trials.
$\text{Estimated probability} = \frac{4}{10}$
$= \frac{2}{5}$
